placeholders.gpx: the pixel count in gigapixels, e.g. 2.684

big.confirm.where: the confirmation shown when starting the very largest render

big.extreme.where: label on the second toggle, which unlocks the single largest export width

big.once.where: label on the third and last export-size tick, nested under Extreme. Opens the sizes past the 65535 that Chrome's canvas limit imposes on the PNG path - 131072 and 262144 - which only the tiled TIFF path can produce, since it streams tiles and never allocates a canvas that wide. Named for the tier's character rather than for any one size in it: the tick does not persist, so it is a decision taken again each time

big.large.where: label on the toggle that unlocks the export widths above 16384, in the File section

big.mem-rec.where: hardware recommendation for the Extreme export tier, beside its tickbox and in its confirmation dialogue

placeholders.gb: what navigator.deviceMemory reports: rounded, and capped by some browsers

big.mem-reported.where: follows the recommendation when the browser reports a memory figure

big.mem-unknown.where: follows the recommendation when the browser reports no memory figure at all

placeholders.mb: the megabytes this render may allocate on this device

big.mem-budget.where: appended to the memory note, stating what the planner will actually take

placeholders.px: the width above which the export stops using a single canvas

big.note-tiled.where: note under the tier toggles when TIFF is chosen, where the export renders a grid of tiles rather than bands

placeholders.px: the width above which the export streams in bands, 16384

big.note.where: standing note beside the Large render toggle once it is on

big.warn.where: the warning shown, and confirmed, when Large render is switched on

big.warn-once.where: the dialog shown when the one-off tick is set. Gives the MEASURED cost of both sizes it opens, that they are TIFF only, what it costs to open one afterwards (slowly, by paging, not never), and that the detail does not run out at any size - so the honest stopping point is what the output can show rather than what the field has left

exp.err.dim.where: error when a tile DID fit and was rendered, but came back short of the light, so the render was refused. Distinct from exp.err.tile, which is about memory: this one must not read as a memory message, because the cause is the blur failing above a certain canvas size

exp.err.floor.where: error when the device can only manage tiles too small to carry the bloom, so the render would finish and be dim rather than fail

exp.err.blank.where: error when a tile came back with nothing drawn on it twice running, so the render is stopped rather than written with holes

sl.glass-cords.where: slider: how strongly the canes of colour show. 0 is clear glass

sl.glass-cordN.where: slider: how many different cane colours were laid into the melt, 2 to 6

sl.glass-cordScale.where: slider: how many canes there are across the sheet

sl.glass-cordWander.where: slider: how much the cane boundaries bend. A hand-drawn cane wanders; a perfectly straight one reads as print

lay.glass-a.where: colour token: the first cane of coloured glass

lay.glass-b.where: colour token: the second cane of coloured glass

lay.glass-c.where: colour token: the third cane of coloured glass

lay.glass-d.where: colour token: the fourth cane of coloured glass

sl.glass-cordLay.where: slider: the angle the canes were laid at ON THE ROD, before any forming. 0 runs them along the rod, 90 wraps them around it

sl.glass-cordTwist.where: slider: how much the gather was twisted about its own axis, which turns a straight cane into a helix

sl.glass-cordLap.where: slider: how far each cane laps over its neighbour. Where they lap the light passes through both, so the seam goes darker - they stack, they never blend

ui.lay-along.where: slider value: the canes run along the rod

ui.lay-around.where: slider value: the canes wrap around the rod

ui.twist-none.where: slider value: the gather was not twisted

ui.lap-butted.where: slider value: the canes meet edge to edge with no overlap

sl.glass-opacity.where: slider: how much of the thickness shows through. At 0 the sheet is a tint you read the form through; at 1 it is solid opal glass and the thickness stops showing at all

ui.opq-clear.where: slider value at 0: the glass is see-through

ui.opq-opal.where: slider value at 1: the glass is solid opal, not see-through at all

lbl.mould.where: label for the choice of mould: what shape the compartments were that the colour was poured into, before anything was done to it

mould.strips.where: button: the mould was parallel strips

mould.radial.where: button: the mould was wedges about the centre, like a crown roundel

lbl.ops.where: heading for the list of operations done to the glass after it was poured. The ORDER matters and the label has to say so

op.spin.where: name of an operation in the list: the outside is dragged round more than the centre

op.blow.where: name of an operation in the list: everything spreads out from the centre

op.roll.where: name of an operation in the list: stretched one way and squeezed the other

op.stir.where: name of an operation in the list: the moon tool dragged through the melt

op.add-spin.where: button: add a spin to the end of the list

op.add-blow.where: button: add a blow to the end of the list

op.add-roll.where: button: add a roll to the end of the list

op.add-stir.where: button: add a stir to the end of the list

ui.ops-empty.where: shown when the list is empty: the glass was poured and left alone, which is a real and useful state, not an error

ui.op-stir-note.where: shown beside a stir in the list instead of an amount slider: a stir has no amount of its own, it takes the moon tool's own settings

a11y.op-up.where: accessible name: move this operation earlier in the order

a11y.op-down.where: accessible name: move this operation later in the order

a11y.op-remove.where: accessible name: remove this operation from the list

mould.cells.where: button: the mould was authored compartments, each with its own width, length and colour

sl.glass-mw.where: slider: the width of the mould's unit cell, in feet. Each compartment's width is a multiple of this

sl.glass-ml.where: slider: the length of the mould's unit cell, in feet. Each compartment's length is a multiple of this

ui.cells-empty.where: shown when the compartment list is empty

cell.add.where: button: add a compartment to the mould

a11y.cell-w.where: accessible name for a compartment's width field, measured in units of the cell width W

a11y.cell-l.where: accessible name for a compartment's length field, measured in units of the cell length L

a11y.cell-colour.where: accessible name: step this compartment to the next colour

lay.glass-e.where: colour token: the fifth glass colour

lay.glass-f.where: colour token: the sixth glass colour

lay.spec-tint.where: colour token: the colour a metal highlight reflects. Gold by default; also serves silver, copper, bronze

sl.glass-oblong.where: slider: how rounded a laid ribbon is. At 0 it has square corners, at 1 its ends are semicircles. A rolled ribbon is between the two, and this is what keeps the joins between colours from coming out as straight facets

sl.glass-start.where: slider: how much thicker than the finished sheet each ribbon starts, as a multiple. A ribbon spreads until it is down to target thickness and then has nothing left to press, so this decides how far it can invade an empty space. At 1 it cannot move at all

ui.ob-square.where: slider value at 0: the ribbon has square corners

ui.ob-stadium.where: slider value at 1: the ribbon's ends are semicircles

ui.start-none.where: slider value at 1: the ribbon starts at target thickness, so there is nothing left to press and it cannot spread

mould.blobs.where: button: the mould was blobs of glass dropped on the sheet, like cookies on a tray, which spread and interweave

sl.glass-blobJit.where: slider: how far each blob wanders off its place on the tray. At 0 they sit on a dead grid and look like one

ui.jit-grid.where: slider value at 0: the blobs sit on an unvaried grid

tool.roller.where: button: the roller tool, drawn as a pass across the slab

toolhint.roller.where: the roller tool's hint. Keep that the roller's circumference IS the repeat and that leaning ACROSS the pass is what tilts it - leaning along it does nothing, and a reader who misses that will think the control is broken on a curve

sl.rollD.where: slider: the roller's diameter in inches. It sets the repeat, because C = pi*D - it is not a pitch chosen directly

sl.rollFace.where: slider: how wide the roller is across, in feet. Wider than the glass and the stamps near its ends miss the piece

sl.rollStampN.where: slider: how many stamps are set around the roller. They are spread evenly, so the angle between them is 360 divided by this, and staggered along the face so no two share a track

sl.rollStampSize.where: slider: how wide each stamp is, in inches

sl.rollStampRot.where: slider: how far the stamp itself is turned, in degrees. The star's own orientation, not where it sits on the roller

sl.rollBite.where: slider: how deep the roller presses. Pressure multiplies this rather than replacing it, so it still works with a mouse

note.roller.where: the roller panel's note: C = pi*D is the repeat, the stamps are staggered, the pass starts with one stamp down, a short piece never sees a full turn, and what pressure and tilt do

hint.roll-the-roller-across.where: shown when a roller pass was too short to be a pass

op.press.where: name of an operation in the list: a drawn roller pass. It presses a pattern in; it does not stretch the sheet, which is what the Roll operation does

opt.source-auto.where: first option in the tile-source select: leave this tile to the automatic assignment instead of pinning it to one section

note.sections-need-two.where: note under the tile setter when only one section is kept. With one source every tile has the same source by definition, so there is nothing to assign and the motif draws in a single colour - this says why instead of looking broken

note.tile-locked.where: note under the section list when any kept section carries a cut. A cut is a box in slab units measured against a particular tile pattern, size and kerf; changing those afterwards reinterprets the same box against a different shape, which renders without error and is wrong. The three controls are disabled until the sections are cleared

ui.op-press-note.where: shown beside a press in the operation list instead of an amount: a drawn pass takes its settings from the roller panel at the moment it was drawn, not from a slider in the list

sec.unnamed.where: default name for a section kept from the slab - a source the floor can be laid from. Sections can be different materials from each other

placeholders.pat: the tiling pattern's own slug, e.g. rhombus - an identifier, never translated

sec.snagged.where: default name for a section taken from a single tile: that one piece of stone, at the coordinates it was cut from, reusable as a source the floor is laid from

sec.kept-cut.where: name given to a section converted from a slab saved when these were wood-only kept cuts

mat.glass.where: button: switch the slab to the glass material

sec.glass.where: section heading for the glass controls

lbl.forming.where: label: which process formed this sheet

a11y.glass-form.where: accessible name for the forming-process buttons

glass.rolled.where: button: sheet formed by rolling, which presses a texture into one face

glass.spun.where: button: crown glass, spun flat from a blown bubble

glass.blown.where: button: cylinder glass, blown long then split and opened flat

glass.poured.where: button: cast or poured glass, which was never drawn in any direction

glass.flat.where: button: a cylinder reheated and flattened

ui.glass-note.where: explains the glass model in one block: a colour field poured into a mould, then an ORDERED list of warps. The order is the load-bearing idea and must survive translation. Also says the forming buttons are presets rather than modes, what each warp does, that the field is thickness, and that nothing is refracted yet

sl.glass-thick.where: slider: nominal sheet thickness in millimetres

sl.glass-tint.where: slider: how much iron is in the melt, which is what makes glass green down its edge

sl.glass-paneX.where: slider: where across the formed disc or cylinder this pane was cut from, in feet

sl.glass-paneY.where: slider: where down the formed disc or cylinder this pane was cut from, in feet

sl.glass-formR.where: slider: the radius of the spun disc, in feet

sl.glass-ream.where: slider: how strong the thickness waviness the forming left behind is

sl.glass-reamScale.where: slider: how fine that waviness is

sl.glass-flutePitch.where: slider: how many flutes the roller pressed in, per foot

sl.glass-fluteDepth.where: slider: how deep those flutes are

sl.glass-seeds.where: slider: how many bubbles are trapped in the melt. A bubble is a void, so it thins the sheet

sl.glass-seedStretch.where: slider: how far the forming drew those bubbles out along its own direction

sl.glass-incl.where: slider: unmelted batch and stones in the melt. Unlike a bubble these thicken the sheet

sl.glass-relief.where: slider: how strongly the slope of the thickness reads as light and dark bands

mat.wood.where: a material choice button; the wood path - sawn timber, not a tree

note.floor-planks.where: the note under the Floor planks sliders. It says these three shape the plank-run pattern only, and that the control for HOW MANY boards the floor is cut from lives elsewhere (Boards, under Tiles & floor) and applies to every pattern. Written because all four sat in one block and the one actually doing the work read as a plank setting

sec.floor-planks.where: section heading in the right-hand rail, directly under Tiles & floor, and shown only for wood. It holds the three controls that shape the plank-run pattern

sec.tiles-and-floor.where: title of a collapsible section in the right-hand rail

sec.wood.where: heading of the wood settings panel

sl.crossT.where: slider in Coat & light: how far along the crossfade the light sits, 0 at the first stop and 1 at the second

sl.specMetal.where: slider beside Specular. At 0 the highlight is the light's own colour, which is how a dielectric - stone, glass, varnish - behaves. At 1 it is the metal tint's colour instead, which is how a metal behaves, and is most of what makes gold read as gold rather than as yellow paint

sl.tedge.where: in the "tiles" group/panel, under the "tiles-and-floor" section

sl.tgrout.where: in the "tiles" group/panel, under the "tiles-and-floor" section

sl.tkerf.where: in the "tiles" group/panel, under the "tiles-and-floor" section

sl.chev-angle.where: slider in Floor planks: the angle the chevron's planks are mitred at, in degrees. 45 is the standard. It is the angle of the CUT across the end of the board, not the angle the floor is laid at

sl.tsize.where: in the "tiles" group/panel, under the "tiles-and-floor" section

sl.wood-plane.where: slider: how far the saw plane stands from the log's axis. Low is quartersawn, high is plainsawn - this one control is the whole range of cuts

sl.wood-y0.where: slider: where along the saw plane the board is taken from

sl.wood-glaze.where: slider in the Wood panel. WOOD-LOOK PORCELAIN: a ceramic tile printed with a wood graphic and finished with a clear glaze - a real and common product, not a trick. Above zero the floor is a TILE, so grout comes back where bare boards have none, and the glaze reads as one sheen across the whole face. At zero it is bare wood

sl.wood-wid.where: slider in the Wood panel: the width of the BOARD cut from the log, in FEET. The plank run inherits it, so it is also how wide a plank is. NOT the same control as sl.wood-plankLen

sl.wood-len.where: slider in the Wood panel: the length of the BOARD cut from the log, in FEET. NOT the same control as sl.wood-plankLen, which is how long the run cuts each plank, in inches. Both were called 'Plank length' once and must not be given the same name again

lbl.board-inches.where: label on two number boxes beside the Plank width and Plank length sliders. The sliders step 0.12 and 0.6 of an inch, which cannot land on a real board figure, and a board is quoted in inches anyway; these take the dimensions directly

a11y.board-len-in.where: accessible name for the board length number box, in inches

a11y.board-wid-in.where: accessible name for the board width number box, in inches

sl.wood-cutAngle.where: slider: which way round the trunk the saw plane faces, in degrees. 0 to 179, because 180 is the same plane cut from the other side

sl.wood-treeDia.where: slider: the log's diameter in feet. A readout you can drag — it shows the size the rings actually came to, and dragging solves once for the ring-width scale rather than pinning the size

lbl.kept-cuts.where: label: the group of saved board cuts the floor is laid from

lbl.sections.where: label on the Sections group: the sources a floor is laid from, each a whole slab and possibly a different material

lbl.tile-source.where: label above the tile setter: a small picture of the pattern's motif where you click a tile and choose which section it is cut from

a11y.wood-set.where: accessible name for the kept-cuts button group

a11y.sections.where: accessible name for the Sections button group

a11y.section-name.where: accessible name for the text field that renames a section in the list

a11y.tile-source.where: accessible name for the select that binds the clicked tile to a section

tool.keep-cut.where: button: save the board currently shown, so the floor is laid from it and any others kept

tool.keep-tile.where: button in the Sections group. Arms the Snag tool: tap a laid tile and that one piece becomes a section, at the coordinates it was cut from. The same thing the Snag tool in the rail does, put where the sections are

tool.add-saved.where: button in the Sections group: open a saved slab file and add it to the set as a section, WITHOUT loading it over the slab you are working on. Load replaces everything including the section list, which makes composing a floor from several saved materials impossible

tool.clear-cuts.where: button: discard every kept cut and go back to cutting one log

tool.build-composite.where: button: re-cut the composite floor from its kept sections. Only shown with two or more sections

tip.build-composite.where: tooltip on the Build composite button, explaining that the floor is not rebuilt automatically while sections are kept

placeholders.n: how many cuts are now kept, e.g. 3

hint.cut-kept.where: status shown after keeping a cut

hint.cuts-cleared.where: status after discarding every kept cut

placeholders.n: how many sections are left, e.g. 3

hint.section-dropped.where: status shown after deleting one section from the list

placeholders.name: the added slab's name, e.g. Carrara
placeholders.mat: its material: stone, wood or glass
placeholders.n: how many sections there are now, e.g. 3

hint.section-added.where: status after adding a saved slab to the set as a section

hint.snag-needs-tiles.where: status when Snag is used while the floor is not laid as tiles

hint.snag-tap-a-tile.where: status when a Snag tap misses every tile

hint.picking-shows-the-slab.where: status when the Snag tool is armed. While picking, the floor shows the live slab rather than the composed sections, so every tap selects from the original material instead of from the floor already built out of earlier picks

placeholders.n: how many sections are now kept, e.g. 3

hint.snag-took.where: status shown after snagging a tile

hint.cuts-full.where: status when trying to keep a ninth cut

sl.wood-plankWid.where: slider in Floor planks: how wide the plank run cuts each floorboard, in INCHES. The floorboard is cut OUT of the mother board, whose own width is sl.wood-wid in feet - this is the size chosen, that one is the material available. A standard floorboard is about 8 inches

sl.wood-plankLen.where: slider in Floor planks: how long the plank run cuts each plank, in INCHES. NOT the same control as sl.wood-len, which is the length of the board it is cut FROM, in feet. Keep the two names distinct

sl.wood-plankVary.where: slider: how much plank lengths differ from the nominal, 0 = all identical

sl.wood-plankStagger.where: slider: how far each row's end joints shift from the row below, 0 = joints stack into columns

tile.pat.chevron.where: a floor layout in the Tiles row, wood only, beside Plank run. CHEVRON: planks mitred at an angle so their ends butt against a mirrored plank and the courses run unbroken in a V. Distinct from herringbone, where the planks meet at a right angle and are NOT mitred - Italian distinguishes these as 'spina ungherese' (chevron) and 'spina di pesce' (herringbone), so do not translate them to the same phrase

tile.pat.plank.where: button: the plank-run floor layout, rows of varying-length boards with staggered end joints

sl.wood-trunkH.where: slider: the whole tree's height from stump to apex, in feet

sl.wood-dEarly.where: slider: multiplier on the bad-year rate during the tree's first years. Early droughts mark the butt, because the tree was only that big

sl.wood-dMid.where: slider: multiplier on the bad-year rate through the tree's middle life

sl.wood-dLate.where: slider: multiplier on the bad-year rate in the tree's last years. Late droughts mark every height, because the tree was full size

sl.wood-flare.where: slider: how much wider the same year's ring is laid at the stump than higher up - the butt swell

sl.wood-flareH.where: slider: the height over which the basal flare dies out, in feet

sl.wood-taper.where: slider: how hard the leader's yearly height increment tracks that year's ring width. 0 means it was always at full height, so the trunk is a cylinder

sl.wood-zBase.where: slider: how far up the trunk this board was cut, in feet above the stump

ui.wood-taper-note.where: explains that a trunk narrows because higher wood has FEWER rings, not thinner ones

sl.wood-fireAt.where: slider: the ring the tree burned in. 0 means it never burned

sl.wood-fireSeverity.where: slider: how much of the cambium the fire killed, 0 to 1

sl.wood-fireWidth.where: slider: the angular width of the killed sector, in degrees

sl.wood-fireAngle.where: slider: which way the wound faces, in degrees

sl.wood-fireHeal.where: slider: how many rings the surviving wood took to close over the wound

sl.wood-fireZ.where: slider: how far up the butt the scar reaches, in feet

ui.wood-fire-note.where: explains that a fire kills cambium on one side only, leaving a buried lens with a charred face

sl.wood-dev2Rise.where: slider: how steeply the branch climbs away from the trunk, in degrees. 0 is straight out horizontally

sl.wood-dev2Prune.where: slider: how the branch ended. 0 it died on the tree and was buried in its own bark, a loose knot; 1 it was taken off clean and healed sound, a tight knot

sl.wood-graft.where: slider: which kept cut the branch grew from. 0 is the tree's own wood; any other and the knot is a different species with its own rings

sec.wood-cut.where: section heading: the controls that place the saw in the log

sec.wood-tree.where: section heading: the whole tree - its height, taper, flare and size

sec.wood-growth.where: section heading: the ring series and the years that made it

sec.wood-figure.where: section heading: fibre direction, the optical figure, and mineral stain

sec.wood-eyes.where: section heading: bird's eye, the point dimples in the cambium

sec.wood-pith.where: section heading: how the pith leans and wanders up the trunk

sec.wood-colour.where: section heading: colour drift along the rings, and the heartwood front

sec.wood-waves.where: section heading: the wave family that makes rings depart from true circles

sec.wood-lobe.where: section heading: an eccentric swelling in the trunk

sec.wood-branch.where: section heading: the branch, its knot, its life and any graft

sec.wood-fire.where: section heading: fire years and the scars they leave

sl.wood-stage.where: slider: how many different boards of the one log the floor is cut from. 1 repeats a single board; higher walks down the cant

sl.wood-rings.where: slider: how many growth rings the log has

sl.wood-late.where: slider: how dark the latewood band is - the contrast of the grain

sl.wood-lean.where: slider: how far the pith leans along the saw plane

sl.wood-leanFine.where: slider: a faster ripple on top of the pith's lean

sl.wood-wander.where: slider: how far the pith wanders across the board

sl.wood-wanderFine.where: slider: a faster ripple on top of the pith's wander

sl.wood-drift.where: slider: how far the colour wanders between the pith and the bark

sl.wood-driftRings.where: slider: how many rings the colour takes to wander that far - the correlation length, not a count of anything

sl.wood-sapRings.where: slider: how many rings inward from the bark are still sapwood - a count of rings, not a distance

sl.wood-sapFade.where: slider: how many rings the conversion from sapwood to heartwood takes - how abrupt the boundary looks

sl.wood-devAmp.where: slider: how far the growth rings bulge away from being circles

sl.wood-devAngle.where: slider: which way round the trunk the bulge points, in degrees

sl.wood-devSpread.where: slider: how much of the trunk's circumference the bulge covers - narrow is a lump, wide is a lean

sl.wood-devStart.where: slider: the ring at which the bulge begins to form. Everything inside it stays round

sl.wood-devRamp.where: slider: how many rings the bulge takes to come fully on

sl.wood-dev2Amp.where: slider: how far the trunk swells where a branch leaves it

sl.wood-dev2Angle.where: slider: which way round the trunk the branch points, in degrees

sl.wood-dev2Spread.where: slider: how much of the trunk's circumference the branch disturbs

sl.wood-dev2Z.where: slider: where ALONG the trunk the branch sits - the control that makes it a branch and not a lean

sl.wood-dev2ZSpan.where: slider: how far along the trunk the branch's influence reaches either side

sl.wood-dev2Start.where: slider: the ring at which the branch begins. Wood inside it is untouched

sl.wood-dev2Ramp.where: slider: how many rings the branch takes to come fully on

sl.wood-dev2Knot.where: slider: how fast the branch cone widens, which sets how big the knot face is. 0 draws no face

sl.wood-dev2KnotPitch.where: slider: how tight the branch's own growth rings are inside the knot face

sl.wood-dev2Die.where: slider: the ring at which the branch died. 0 means it is still alive, so the knot runs to the bark; any other value stops it there and the trunk grows over it

sl.wood-waveAmp.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-waveK.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-waveZ.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-anchorAt.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-anchorOver.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-anchorTo.where: slider: part of the shared wave family that makes a tree a species

sl.wood-juv.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-decay.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-floor.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-vary.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-dRate.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-dDepth.where: slider: part of the growth curve - how a species puts on width over its life

sl.wood-lateFrac.where: slider: what fraction of each ring is the dark latewood band

sl.wood-lateSharp.where: slider: how abruptly the latewood begins - sharp in a fir, soft in a maple

sl.wood-mineral.where: slider: how strongly mineral stain shows. Colour only - the wood is sound, just discoloured

sl.wood-mineralSize.where: slider: what share of the cross-section stains. The field scale sets how wide a streak is; this sets how many

sl.wood-mineralSpacing.where: slider: how far apart the streaks sit in the cross-section, in inches

lay.wood-mineral.where: colour token: the mineral stain colour, grey-green by default

sl.wood-gloss.where: slider: how strongly fibre direction shows as light and dark at all. 0 draws no figure

sl.wood-fibreSpiral.where: slider: a steady helical wind of the fibres about the trunk, in degrees

sl.wood-interlock.where: slider: how far the spiral angle swings when it alternates - interlocked grain, which is what gives ribbon figure

sl.wood-interlockRings.where: slider: how many years the spiral takes to reverse and come back

sl.wood-curl.where: slider: how far the fibres undulate across the trunk - fiddleback and quilt

sl.wood-curlRate.where: slider: how tightly that undulation repeats along the trunk

sl.wood-eyes.where: slider: how strongly the bird's-eye dimples show. 0 draws none

sl.wood-eyeSpacing.where: slider: how far apart the dimples sit on the cambium

sl.wood-eyeSize.where: slider: how wide each eye is, in inches

sl.wood-eyeDepth.where: slider: how far the growth rings dip into a dimple - the dip is what makes the little concentric circles

placeholders.n: how many tiles the pattern sets around each centre, so how many sections it needs
placeholders.have: how many sections the user has kept so far

hint.rosette-wants.where: shown when a rosette pattern is chosen but there are too few sections to fill its slots without repeating one inside a motif. {n} is how many sections the pattern needs, {have} is how many the user has kept. It falls back to a plain cut rather than doubling one up

placeholders.have: how many sections are kept, e.g. 3
placeholders.alt: the name of the other grouping, already translated, e.g. Hexagon
placeholders.altn: tiles that other grouping needs, e.g. 3

hint.grouping-smaller-fits.where: status when there are too few sections for the chosen grouping but enough for another one the pattern offers

tool.stack.where: the middle of three assembly orders, beside In order and Shuffled. The floor is cut from one board and then assembled, and this is the installer working out of the PILE rather than following the numbered guide: pieces leave the machine in cut order across the board and are laid in lay order across the floor, so when the floor is not the board those two orders drift apart. Systematic and repeatable, not random - that is Shuffled

tool.shuffle.where: in the "Tile options" group/panel, under the "tiles-and-floor" section
